- She took the 9-5 evenings easier to rest, and came back in a better place. Rob called this the most realistic story of building online for the first time, especially around a job: "She's human just like you and I are."
- Her app logs mood plus habits. After 14 days of logging it surfaces "early patterns" from a statistical calculation, with habit streaks and a calendar view.
- Her takeaway: the six weeks strengthened her wish to do entrepreneurship outside the 9-5, and she plans to keep going "with or without" the show.
- Rob's point: progress is incremental, so rest and keep going rather than quit.

chunks.heading: Pivoting when nobody buys: Davis's story
chunks.text:
- Davis had built products before but never made a dollar. His first app (Daily Sensei) got no buyers, so he pivoted to a productized, automated service: hosting an OpenClaw server for people who want one without setting it up.
- Pricing used Rob's launch method: $19.99/month for the first 10 customers, with the full price set higher at $100/month. Only one plan.
- He had an insight to pre-build servers in advance rather than build one each time someone pays.
- He stopped posting online and DMed people in communities and people asking for OpenClaw help. More than 50 conversations produced 1 customer ($19.99/month). He called it "a painful sale" of manual, brutal outreach.
- The one-on-one conversations showed why people did not buy. The biggest reason was trust (what happens to my server if you shut down?). Others: not ready to pay $20/month, and people not replying.
- Posting on X got attention but no payment; direct outreach got a sale.
- He launched two products in six weeks, and the original app was still stuck in App Store review.
- Rob's takeaway: the first idea usually does not work. People say they want something but will not put money behind it. Listen to the market, talk to users, set your ego aside, pivot, and stick with it.

chunks.heading: Cold outreach to local businesses: Meraj's sales process
chunks.text:
- Meraj, 18, built a tool that turns a website URL into a finished social carousel (Super X is a similar product), fully on autopilot. The only input is the URL.
- He sourced leads from Google Maps. He filtered out businesses unlikely to pay and kept ones that already had an Instagram page or website, since those owners care about marketing. He also chose businesses whose offerings are pricey enough to justify marketing spend, even at about $10 in the Indian context.
- He did not ask for the sale in the first message, only for a yes. He told owners he had already made a sample post and full plan for them and asked if they wanted to see it. Saying yes costs them nothing; the worst case is they dislike it and block him.
- Most did not reply. One engaged, and he got 1,500 rupees (about $15) as his first sale. Within weeks he made $64.90 total, including a $50 sale from one person and then a second $50 sale.
- Rob called this "a master class": find leads, open with value, then show a result built from their own business. Rob noted the carousels looked so good he first assumed they were made by hand.
- His early setback: a gym owner rejected him, he improved the product and came back. Rob said Meraj showed up with force after a sick period and heavy online criticism.

chunks.heading: Persistence and confidence
chunks.text:
- Meraj lost accountability after the weekly calls stopped, doubted himself, and feared not winning his bet against himself. His advice: "it's okay to be also a bit delusional as long as you're not like too delusional," and "stay delusional." If he had quit three weeks earlier because of the gym owner, he would not have this story.
- Rob's closing lesson: if you keep going you will achieve what you want. All three were rejected several times and still started, shipped and sold.
- Rob's observation on audience: some viewers follow the series closely, and he is reminded of that when strangers approach his participants at events.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob checks in on three people given 6 weeks and a $100 budget to earn their first online dollar. He reviews their week-one landing pages and advises: build in a domain you know, talk to users to shape your packaging, and sell outcomes rather than features. He also covers a viral backlash against one participant and the difference between client income and product income.

chunks.heading: The "First Dollar" challenge setup
chunks.text:
- Rob recruited three people for a challenge: 6 weeks and a $100 budget to build something from scratch and make their first dollar online.
- Week one task: build a landing page in 48 hours.
- Week two task: get someone actually paying. Not a friend, not a free user, but a real paying customer who also gives valuable feedback.
- Rob defines "first dollar" strictly: money from a product the person built and sold themselves, not income from working for other people.
- He says the deadline pressure matters. One participant said having Rob set weekly timelines "is way more different" than self-imposed ones and has "really helped me progress with the pace."

chunks.heading: Build in an area you know, or at least care about
chunks.text:
- Rob would advise 99% of founders to stay in an area they are expert in.
- Reasoning: an expert builds with the least effort a product that is "so much better than everybody else" in that field, and is self-motivated to build and scale it.
- He agrees with a participant (a finance-industry veteran) who refused a suggested business helping young people break into finance. The participant had left that industry for personal reasons and wasn't interested in recruitment.
- His rule: if it's something you don't care about or aren't interested in, passing is fair. Honest answers about what you actually believe are better than chasing a "logical" idea.

chunks.heading: Validate the idea with real people before building
chunks.text:
- One participant (Daily Sensei) planned a Telegram bot teaching AI daily to non-technical solo founders.
- He posted in groups asking for feedback. The main objection was not the idea but the channel: Telegram isn't widely used by non-technical people.
- The idea morphed into an iPhone app, with payment through the Apple ecosystem so people "don't feel that they're paying" (just a double tap).
- The landing page went live at dailysensei.com with a waitlist.
- He ran an open call meetup in Latvia: 170 people applied for 30 spots. He plans to send the MVP to those applicants first.
- Rob's takeaway across the participants: talk to users first, use the feedback to adjust the landing page and product.

chunks.heading: Pricing: charge more from the start
chunks.text:
- The Daily Sensei builder said he likes the idea of charging more from the start but that charging more is "a big mental block."
- He also had a fixation on getting somebody to pay exactly $1.
- The source shows the block, not Rob's counsel on it. Rob's own stated rule here is simply that the goal is a real paying customer.

chunks.heading: Landing page packaging: outcomes over functionality
chunks.text:
- Rob's critique of the "Cadenza" landing page (a SaaS for small business owners' social media publishing cadence): the headline "Generates a week of Instagram posts in 60 seconds" is functionality-focused.
- His fix: make it outcome focused. Ask "why do I care about generating a week of Instagram posts?" The answer (building social presence to drive customers) is what to lead with.
- His reasoning: "All the businesses care about is more money."
- A business's success depends on delivering results, but also on getting users in the door and setting expectations for those results, which is "having the right packaging."
- Rob says the packaging should be tested with users rather than assumed good.

chunks.heading: Reddit for early feedback
chunks.text:
- The Cadenza builder stitched the landing page together from components and templates found online.
- Rob endorsed his plan to use Reddit and speak to small business owners to get critical feedback on initial reception, then fine-tune the landing page and product accordingly.
- Rob called it important to commit to speaking to users to adjust the landing page.

chunks.heading: Controversy and attention
chunks.text:
- A clip from episode one went viral. It showed a participant (18 years old) describing 12 Codex subscriptions running 10 agents in parallel, and critics said he was wasting money and not building anything real. A large streamer commented on it live to about 2,500 people.
- Context Rob gave: the participant has multiple clients for whom he builds free SEO tools at scale, ranks them on Google, and earns more than the rest of his household combined.
- Rob distinguishes this client income from the challenge goal, which is revenue from his own product.
- The viral attention brought inbound requests from people wanting SEO growth help.
- Rob told him "who cares what these people are saying" given he supports his family. The participant's view: attention can't be orchestrated, "all I can do is show up and stay true to myself."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam explains why he failed for nearly two years building original ideas, then succeeded by cloning a proven product (an X post scheduler) and making one part 10x better. He gives three practical validation routes (copy a proven idea, sell a service first, put a buy button on a landing page) and argues builders should ride existing market waves instead of creating demand.

chunks.heading: Rob's core thesis: validation is money, and don't create waves, ride them
chunks.text:
- Rob argues that with AI you can build almost anything, so the question is no longer "what can you build" but "what should you build".
- His definition: "Validation is money." Unless building is a hobby, asking a friend "do you like my product idea?" is useless. Ask "would you buy it?"
- He calls opinions "a courtesy" and not a basis for a business.
- His surf analogy: one person flails in the ocean trying to make their own waves; the other is calm and waits for the inevitable wave. The product is the surfboard, and the money is the water.
- Rob says he was the flailing person for years. Reinventing the wheel is "the worst thing you can do" if you want a business that pays your bills and gives you freedom.
- Unless you are a multi-billion-dollar fund that can create demand and move a market, creating a wave is not your job. Spend time in the market, watch the trends, then ride them.
- He ends with: stop asking people whether they would pay, and get them to pay. "Put the buy button."

chunks.heading: Rob's failure history before validating
chunks.text:
- In August 2024 he posted on X about his failures. It took him 1 year and 11 months of attempts with no result. He had no agency and had made no money.
- Failed projects he lists: Coach Miro (connecting coaches with each other or with clients), Indie Hackers (a platform to help indie builders connect), and a luxury-apartments directory.
- His diagnosis: he was trying to build things that didn't exist yet (no directory for X), which means trying to make waves himself.
- The tweet that went viral was about failing repeatedly. He joked that after 26 more failures you would statistically be a winner, and says the real number turned out not to be 26.

chunks.heading: Playbook 1: Copy a proven idea and make one part 10x better
chunks.text:
- Use a directory of proven ideas such as TrustMRR (made by a person named Mark on X). It lists business ideas that are proven because they earn revenue and shows how much each earns. Logging in gives more data.
- Pick one, run it through AI, and make it your own, but make one part ten times better.
- Example: Nevo David and Postiz, a social media post scheduler. Schedulers like Buffer and Hootsuite had existed for decades and make roughly $2-3 million a month. Nevo struggled at first, then changed course to improve one part of the scheduler 10x: exposing it to AI agents.
- Rob says Postiz went from about $17-20K a month roughly four months earlier to about $140K a month, within about three months, from that single change.
- He used the same method for his own product, Super X, an X (Twitter) post scheduler and growth tool.
  - Existing proven products: Tweet Hunter (his co-founder's old product, about $150K a month, and about $250K a month when his co-founder sold it), Hypefury and Typefully.
  - His "10x better" angle was improving the AI integrations 10x.
- The risk shifts. With an unproven idea the risk is whether anyone wants it. With a proven idea the risk moves to execution, which is "completely within your control."

chunks.heading: Playbook 2: Sell a service first, then build the product
chunks.text:
- Example: his friend Roman and his startup Gojiberry, an AI lead-finding platform (also spelled "Goji Berry" in the source). Per Rob, it passed $3M a year.
- How it started: they ran an agency selling lead packages to other companies, validating demand before building any product. It was a normal services agency with about 10-20 clients paying monthly for lead data.
- Benefits Rob names:
  - Cash flow up front, so you don't burn savings.
  - A ready first customer base. You show the product to existing clients and ask what they think.
- Rob says the product then reached $1M a year in about eight months, and about $3M a year after roughly a year and a half. (The source says "within a year, within eight months" for the first milestone.)
- Pricing change: they cut what they charged clients from about $3,000 a month under the agency to $800 a month for the product, which let them serve far more customers.
- He describes the agency as riding a wave with clients while Roman and his co-founders could not yet ride it themselves, so they built the product to do it.

chunks.heading: Playbook 3: Landing page with a buy button (the Levels.io approach)
chunks.text:
- Rob credits Pieter Levels (Levels.io), a prominent indie hacker on X. The method: put up a landing page for an idea and add a buy button. Rob frames it as "show me the money."
- He says Levels made about $100K a month before AI and about $44K a month from remote-work-related projects (the source is unclear on the exact attribution), and more at his peak.
- Rob saved this for last because it combines with the other two: you can add a landing page and a "will you pay for this?" button to a copied idea or a service offer.
- Strategies one and two give you up-front cash flow, or a proven idea, so you don't worry about running out of money.

chunks.heading: Rob's own run, and how he knew it would work
chunks.text:
- About a year before this talk (the video is dated 2026-07-16), he left his home and his job and lived off savings. He tweeted that he was becoming a founder. He calls it "either the smartest or the dumbest decision" of his life.
- He was nervous about hitting his goal of $10K a month, but he knew the core idea was proven because he applied Playbook 1.
- Timeline he gives: roughly six months of hard work with no income, from January (the first post) to July, when he started publicly posting about it. The slow part was building infrastructure, which is complex for something like Super X. After about eight months he reached $10K a month with recurring revenue.
- He says demand grew over that time, because X is gaining users, so the market was expanding.

chunks.heading: Q&A: How do you measure "10x better"?
chunks.text:
- Rob says you can't measure it precisely, unlike AI benchmarks (88.8%, 80%, 89%).
- For Super X he had been using Tweet Hunter and Hypefury and was frustrated. Their AI-generated tweets were "so bad".
- His test: build something he himself wants to use daily, and check whether it is actually better than the product he is comparing against.
- He cautions that "I built it to scratch my own itch" alone is not a validated product idea. Do both: scratch your own itch and others' at the same time.

chunks.heading: Q&A: Paid vs organic traffic, and competing as a copycat
chunks.text:
- Super X growth was 99% organic, mainly his own tweets, because his ICP (X users who want an X scheduler) lives on X.
- He did run paid ads, and they currently lose money on ad spend. Reason: it gives a steady stream of users, so when he changes the product he can watch how trial conversion and churn shift. He pays for a consistent feedback flow, not for growth.
- To compete with incumbents when you copy, he uses a "gravity" analogy: the more mass a brand has, the more pull it creates (the Sun vs the Earth). Create mass by constantly showing up, making noise, shipping updates, announcing news, and sharing customer success stories.
- Same logic for SEO: rank by publishing more high-quality content and earning more backlinks. He says the key is volume of quality content, not time in market.
- His own cadence: posted on X daily, ran a daily video update series for 133 days, and now does it weekly.
- Why this beats incumbents: once big players get comfortable they stop posting and updating, which leaves room for small founders who can move fast and produce a lot of content.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob replied to a Levels.io tweet with an idea, was challenged to build it, and shipped canivibecoded.com open source overnight. A tweet and video brought 35k views and 9k visitors in 48 hours, and sponsor slots sold at $299 to $999 each, reaching about $7.6k/mo. His next problem is keeping traffic high enough to give sponsors ROI.

chunks.heading: How Rob built canivibecoded.com in a few hours from a tweet
chunks.text:
- The idea came from a reply to a tweet by Peter Levels (Levels.io), who had posted about re-engineering projects like WhisperFlow, Granola and Woop.
- Rob replied that someone should build a tool that shows which subscriptions you pay for and which ones you could vibe code yourself.
- Levels answered "It's a great idea. Can you build it?" and Rob started within the hour, around 11pm.
- The product is a web app called canivibecoded.com: a list of tools or subscriptions you can build yourself. Each entry has a prompt you paste into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, so you don't pay (for example) $20 a month.
- Rob bought the domain 19 minutes into the build.
- He decided to make the whole site open source, because he thinks the idea works better that way.
- He wanted it to be easy to use and a bit funny, with a question-style hook such as "Can I vibe code this?" (Resend for sending emails is one example).
- Design was done in Paper, with a separate prompt per page. The site works well on mobile.

chunks.heading: Launch sequence and the time cost
chunks.text:
- Rob stayed up until about 3:45am to finish and ship before sleeping, then recorded a video and posted a tweet around 5am. He had planned to be in bed at 1am.
- He chose to publish immediately instead of waiting, because he wanted it out before he slept.
- Eleven minutes after posting, the tweet had 11 likes. He was unsure it would work: "It could flop, who knows. We'll keep going anyway."
- After waking up, the tweet had 65K views and 34 retweets. A poll on Granola had 23 votes.
- The launch rode on an existing audience built over years on X and through his own brand.

chunks.heading: Early traffic numbers
chunks.text:
- After 48 hours: more than 35K views and 9K visitors.
- After about 3 days: roughly 14K unique visitors and 1,000 prompts copied.
- On day 3, about 5,000 page views from midnight to the time of recording.
- He says retention looks high, and people keep returning to the site.

chunks.heading: Monetizing with sponsorship slots
chunks.text:
- About two days after launch, Rob launched sponsor slots.
- First sponsor: Martin Lasak of Wishkit. He announced it on X, and the second sponsorship came in right after, from Peter's Post Fast.
- Third slot went to Goji Berry. Simon of Founder Stack bought a $599 slot at the same time. At that point he put the run rate at about $1.8K per month.
- Slot prices he mentions across sales: $299, $399, $499, $599, $799 and $999.
- Within about an hour he went from the first slot to roughly $2,000.
- Three more sponsors followed on the Sunday: Posters, Bullseye, and Browser Blast (Indexsy).
- Run rate moved from $0 to $7.6K per month in 48 hours, on a project he started on a Thursday.
- The title claims $9k a month. The transcript only supports the $7.6K per month figure.

chunks.heading: The retention problem and what Rob did next
chunks.text:
- Rob's stated challenge after the spike: keep traffic up so sponsors get a return on investment.
- He says the site seems to be something people revisit, which helps.
- He had already launched a new weekly newsletter as one way to keep visitors coming back.
- He says he has "a lot of ideas" for keeping traffic going but does not detail them.

chunks.heading: Mindset notes on building alone
chunks.text:
- Rob has spent years building his personal brand and posting what he builds. This was the first time something he built got attention on its own.
- He previously built Super X with co-founders, so credit was shared. He says he never knew whether he could have done it alone.
- He argues that confidence changes when you actually do it: "the alignment between what you were always telling yourself and what became concrete reality."
- His advice to people who feel stuck: reaching the top is "just a matter of time".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam argues video is the highest-leverage skill in 2026 and credits it for taking his business to $30,000 a month. He shares seven practical lessons from a year of daily videos: energy, viewer focus, intentional speaking, eye contact, hooks, audio, and captions. The unifying idea is deliberate reps and improving 1% each day.

chunks.heading: Why Rob made video his highest-leverage skill
chunks.text:
- Rob credits video as the reason his business reached $30,000 a month and the reason for the life he lives now.
- He has had multiple videos on X pass 1 million views. One video about his experience in Cyprus did over 700,000 views in a week.
- He started a year before this video by filming with the iPhone front camera. Those videos were basic, and "Nobody watched them."
- His belief: video is the highest-leverage skill to develop in 2026. AI can generate video, but it cannot capture "the human soul part" or replicate stories a person has lived. A 10-20 minute human video about your own experiences has no AI equivalent right now.
- One good video can reach more people than you could meet in a lifetime and open doors you can't predict.
- He says it is not about talent, it is about reps. His framing: choose to "suck 1% less every single day."

chunks.heading: Bring energy by putting in reps and setting up your routine
chunks.text:
- Nobody enjoys watching a flat, sleepy presenter. Energy on camera was one of his hardest early problems because he is a self-described introvert who gets energy from being alone.
- Nobody, Mr. Beast included, is born comfortable talking to a camera. Comfort and energy come only from reps.
- Tactic: find what dials you up.
  - For Rob, caffeine helps, and so does the time of day.
  - He films around sunset, which is why the lighting in his videos looks the same each time.
  - His routine: wake around 11:00 a.m., move his body, eat something filling, have caffeine, work slowly early and ramp up later, then film.
  - A camera in front of him at 11:00 a.m. right after waking "would be horrible."
- Order matters: put in the reps first. Only after that can you record when you feel like it.

chunks.heading: Make the video about the viewer, not yourself
chunks.text:
- Viewers are always asking, often subconsciously, "How is it helping me?"
- Easiest fix: use less "I" and more "you." Frame points as what the viewer can do (for example, "you can make your own videos better by doing X, Y, Z").
- He says the more you make videos about the viewer, the more viewers you get.
- Value does not have to be education. Three kinds of value he names:
  - Entertainment, such as Mr. Beast, who checks the engagement graph on every upload, removes whatever does not perform, never repeats it, and iterates toward highly produced, engaging videos.
  - Education.
  - Connection, by sharing a story vulnerably.
- What is not value: talking without context about your day when nobody knows who you are.
- Before every recording, ask what the viewer gets out of it. This applies to short form and long form.

chunks.heading: Speak with intention, and don't over-polish
chunks.text:
- Viewers give you their time, so respect it. Think about what you'll say before you hit record.
- Rob uses a list of talking points, not a word-for-word script, and then riffs. He cuts the "ums" and "ahs."
- Reps must be intentional. His gym analogy: swinging a dumbbell randomly builds nothing, while learning what a bicep curl targets and thinking about each rep does. Speaking reps work the same way.
- Replace filler words ("um," "uh," "like," "but") with silence. Pausing to think is fine.
- Don't polish too much, especially in long form. Occasional ums, pauses and mistakes make you relatable. Over-cut video puts people off because they can't relate to the person.
- Short form needs more polish than long form, though he notes a trend where less polished, more real videos do better.
- As a benchmark, he points to Higher Up Wellness on Instagram: people who talk naturally for hours with no filler words, which he says is highly engaging. Practice avoiding filler words and it becomes natural.

chunks.heading: Framing: look at the lens, not yourself
chunks.text:
- Talk to the camera at eye level, as if eye to eye with the viewer.
- Don't glance at the preview screen, and don't read a script with your eyes moving across it. Even if viewers don't notice consciously, they pick up on it and it signals you don't believe what you're saying.
- Looking at the camera creates the best connection with the viewer, which makes the video more engaging and therefore more viewed.

chunks.heading: Hooks: the first seconds and the three things to cover
chunks.text:
- Hooks are the most important part for getting people to keep watching.
- Length: about 3 seconds (possibly 2) on short form; 5 to 15 seconds on long form.
- On this video's own hook, Rob says he deliberately covered three things:
  - What you will learn.
  - Why it is worth learning (the return on investment of getting better at video).
  - Why he is qualified, so he isn't "some random guy who's never made a video." Pair good quality with credibility.

chunks.heading: Audio, then captions
chunks.text:
- Sound is the most important part of a video, more than the picture.
  - People will watch grainy camcorder-style video on Instagram if the audio is good, and will scroll past instantly if the audio is bad.
  - Also make the video look decent (lighting matters), but audio comes first.
  - Rob uses the DJI Mic Mini, which clips on and connects to his camera. He says it is not sponsored and is reliable.
- Captions: he cites that approximately 75% of people watch videos on mute (subway, bus, gym, casual scrolling).
  - A video without captions loses those viewers, because they won't turn on sound to find out what you're saying.
  - He calls captions "the single best thing you can do" for retention and viewership.
- Where to use them:
  - Add captions on X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, Threads and any non-YouTube platform.
  - Skip burned-in captions on YouTube. YouTube has auto captions, and many viewers are on TV (which YouTube is pushing heavily), so viewers can turn captions on or off themselves.

chunks.heading: How to improve: one change per video
chunks.text:
- What prompted the video: Rob noticed several small issues in a newer creator's videos, messaged him, and the next video was much better. It showed Rob how much he had picked up from hundreds of daily videos over a year.
- Rob's plan to avoid procrastinating:
  - Pick one point from the list and record a video now, applying it. Options include captions, eye contact or fixing audio.
  - The next day, keep that change and add another.
  - Keep stacking daily. His claim: after 100 videos you will be "completely transformed."
- "It only takes one viral video to change your life."
- He plans more videos on founding startups, making videos and building SaaS products.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam lays out a beginner SEO playbook for new products with no domain authority: show up in LLM retrieval by earning mentions and owning content on LinkedIn, YouTube and your own site. Start with versus, alternatives and review pages, make them unique, and format them so LLMs can summarize them.

chunks.heading: Rob's goal: SEO and AEO playbook for beginners
chunks.text:
- Rob frames the target outcome as an "SEO playbook for beginners to get your first 10 to 15 articles published" so a new product can rank in AI search and Google and start getting customers.
- His premise: "it is easier than ever to build," and the hard part is getting customers for what was built.
- He calls the approach "search everywhere optimization": optimizing for search on Google, LinkedIn, Reddit and YouTube, not just a website.
- He says his playbook helped him bootstrap three companies to multiple millions in revenue.
- He cites a study (company name not recalled) showing roughly 17 times higher conversion from ChatGPT and other LLMs than from Google. His reasoning: people treat LLMs like a personal therapist and trust them.
- His practical timeline for a brand new product: power through the 10 to 15 pieces in about two weeks.

chunks.heading: How a product shows up in AI search: retrieval, not training data
chunks.text:
- Rob names two ways to appear in AI answers: being in the model's training data, or retrieval. Training is hard to influence because models are only retrained occasionally, so he focuses on retrieval.
- Retrieval happens when a prompt forces the LLM to run a web search, such as product comparisons and pricing queries. These are very bottom-of-funnel.
- The flow he describes: user prompt, the LLM turns it into search queries, checks a search engine like Google or Bing, chooses URLs to cite, scrapes and summarizes them, then answers the user.
- His rule: at the stage where the LLM chooses which URLs to cite, you must either show up with your own content or be mentioned on content that already exists.
- You can see the sources behind a ChatGPT answer by opening the sources list at the bottom of the response.

chunks.heading: Four ways to get mentioned on other people's content
chunks.text:
- Identify authoritative sources the LLMs already cite. Reddit is the most obvious.
- Pursue genuine coverage: expert quotes and contributions to pieces already being cited by LLMs. He did this as a journalist.
- Pay to get on listicles. Aim for the top one to three spots on pages like "best payment processing SaaS." If the LLM scrapes and summarizes that listicle, you get recommended.
- Keep your brand description consistent across every site that mentions you, so mentions portray you accurately.
- On paid placements: he says even publications like Forbes can be paid to feature you, which yields a high-quality backlink, and the same mechanism works for AI mentions.

chunks.heading: "Owned mentions" cheat code: rank through LinkedIn and YouTube
chunks.text:
- Most cited domains by AI, per Rob: Reddit first, LinkedIn second, YouTube fourth.
- A new site has no domain authority, so ranking on your own site is hard. Leveraging LinkedIn or YouTube authority can be easier.
- Example: for a hard, bottom-of-funnel keyword ("programmatic SEO 2026" for their agency), his co-founder Jake wrote a LinkedIn Pulse article that ranks number one. It was an experiment, not planned for SEO. A LinkedIn post by Jake was also cited by ChatGPT for the query "Cleo versus Stanley." The team now produces this kind of content for clients.
- Backlinks come from odd places (a Product Hunt comment gave them one). He says links in LinkedIn or YouTube content are good but not worth sweating: write the piece, put it on LinkedIn, and link back to the homepage.
- On YouTube, the bar is low. Using his tool Mentions (tracking a form builder, Tally.so), he shows cited YouTube videos with a watermarked background, slow cadence, and about 117 views and 2 likes. His point: you do not need to be an S-tier YouTuber, you just need a video that is good enough.

chunks.heading: YouTube SEO checklist for being cited
chunks.text:
- Title the video with the target keyword, for example "best form builder 2026."
- Make sure the video has a transcript and closed captions.
- Fill the description with the target keyword plus related secondary keywords (for example "best form builder for professionals"). Make it genuinely descriptive and link back to the page you want to rank.
- Name the thumbnail file with the target keyword.
- Embed the video on the matching landing page on your website. This makes the page more comprehensive and creates a cycle that helps YouTube, AI search and Google.
- If you are reviewing competitors, you can list yourself first, but be fair to them. His review of Stanley used a real signup and screenshots, so crawlers and Google see it as a fair review.

chunks.heading: Which content to write first: versus, alternatives and review pages
chunks.text:
- Rob recommends beginners skip fancy keyword tools and start with three bottom-of-funnel types: "[you] versus [competitor]," "[competitor] alternatives," and "[competitor] review."
- Reason: a user searching you versus a competitor is at the end of the buying journey and just needs a push.
- Proof: his bootstrapped SaaS Cleo (zero funding) ranks number one and number two against VC-funded competitor Stanley, and the AI overview is all Cleo.
- Reviews should be honest: sign up for the competitor's tool and include screenshots. Interlink the review to the versus page, which helps both rank.
- Reviewing competitors lets you ride their existing authority and redirect attention to your product.
- Day-one plan for a newly shipped product: list competitors, create versus, alternatives and review content on your site, then on YouTube and LinkedIn add "best [category]" content (for example "best personal branding tool"). LinkedIn is lower effort: "get in your computer and start writing."
- Reverse-engineer what to write: use a citation tracker (his Mentions tool, or Profound) to see which URLs LLMs cite for your target prompt. Create content at similar URLs, add unique information, and make it better. He did this for client Beehiiv by finding content competitors had that the client lacked.

chunks.heading: Using AI to write content without being a copy of everyone else
chunks.text:
- Rob says you can use Claude for a first draft, but he argues that fully AI-generated content fails: competitors are doing the same thing, and the model just summarizes content already ranking. His logic: "why is any search engine going to rank your content over the source material?"
- Fix: edit as a human and add unique information that is absent from currently ranking pages: first-party or proprietary data, video, testimonials, firsthand experiences.
- Do as many of these as is easy. A brand new tool may lack data but can add a video with firsthand experience and commentary.
- Validation from the host's experience (not Rob's claim, so treated here only as context): content built from his own users' data ranked best. Rob's reaction: "That is a piece of content that only you could create."
- Do not spam: no private blog networks, no spraying brand mentions everywhere. Focus on high-quality content that LLMs use as source material.

chunks.heading: Three phases of AI visibility and how to structure pages
chunks.text:
- Phase 1: check whether you show up and how ChatGPT describes your brand. If positioning is wrong, change the copy on your site and the pages being used as sources.
- Phase 2: compare how you are described versus competitors. Look at their pages being used as sources, copy what works, and make it better.
- Phase 3: appear and be framed as a leader for generic category prompts like "best form builder."
- If pages are indexed but nothing happens, create more content or improve it. LLMs summarize in short, digestible paragraphs, so write that way.
- Include a facts section answering longtail conversational questions (for example "what is the best form builder for building hospital admission forms"). Use H1 and H2 for primary keywords and H3s plus facts for longtail.
- Many users do not read your page; they read the LLM's summary, so write for the summary.

chunks.heading: The 80/20 recipe for your first 10 to 15 articles
chunks.text:
- Map the competition: list content ranking on page one for your target keywords and prompts.
- Audit each for elements (facts section, comparison tables, word count) and for weaknesses such as missing information or no embedded video.
- Match the competition's comprehensiveness, then one-up them as many times as possible. He compares it to tabloid covers: "10 tips" versus "11 tips."
- Add a short, lightweight one-minute video reviewing each tool if competitors lack one.
- Summary checklist: audit AI visibility; track citations and mentions; pursue earned media intentionally (paid listicles, or Reddit posts where the founder contributes useful information); create bottom-of-funnel content; target conversational queries with long variations; add unique content; include LLM-friendly elements (digestible paragraphs, facts, subheadings); one-up competitors.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam describes his solopreneur routine: a night-owl schedule, settling 2-3 months per location, front-loading chores to get an 8-hour flow block, and prioritizing boring high-impact work. He frames building a business as surfing and argues productivity follows happiness, not discipline.

chunks.heading: Rob's daily work routine: night-owl schedule and one deep work block
chunks.text:
- Rob makes $22,000 a month and runs the whole business himself while traveling.
- He lives the "reverse typical guru advice lifestyle". He wakes around 11:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. because he goes to bed late. He is a night owl, not a morning person.
- He felt guilt about this for a while, but says "for me it works".
- Midday he has breakfast, gets some sun, and answers a few customer support emails.
- Around 2 to 3 p.m. he goes to the gym on training days (weights, then cardio), showers and makes coffee.
- He front-loads chores and hard errands so that nothing else is left to do when work starts.
- In the evening, once it is quiet and nobody is texting, he does a full 8-hour solid work block. He says that is how he gets into flow state.

chunks.heading: Rob's rule for choosing what to build: the boring stuff moves the business
chunks.text:
- Rob keeps a running list, reset roughly monthly or every two months. It holds the top three or four features he wants to build, things to improve, and bugs. He notes items as they come up.
- When he sits down, he either continues yesterday's work or picks from the list by feel. He says he is privileged to be able to work on what he wants.
- He tries to focus on what moves the business forward the most. Building his startup taught him what that is, because he tends to want the fun, visual, flashy work.
- His conclusion: "99% of the time the stuff that moves the business forward the most is the boring stuff."
- When a list gets too long, he creates a new note and copies over only the important items.
- If a customer doesn't raise something again, or he forgets it, he treats it as not important enough to begin with.
- Triage signal: a critical bug or real issue generates several emails (for example five), so he knows it matters and gets it done. A one-off request for a small tweak or an extra setting that nobody else asks for gets dropped if he lacks time.
- He admits this may not be the most optimal way of working, but it has worked well so far.

chunks.heading: Building a business is like surfing: get in the water and read the waves
chunks.text:
- Rob's analogy: building a business is like surfing.
- You spend a lot of time in the water watching waves, learning what a wave that will break properly looks like before it breaks. You only learn that from time in the water.
- A solopreneur or small-team founder's job is to pick the big waves, see them coming, get on them and ride them.
- He says this is why people who win once win again and again. The hardest step is getting in the water the first time: the board is new, you must learn the leash, everything is new and overstimulating.
- Once you have been in the water long enough to read waves, catching and riding them stops being a problem. Whether to get off one wave and pick another is up to you.
- His advice: "You just got to get in the water."

chunks.heading: Travel cadence: base for 2 to 3 months, not constant movement
chunks.text:
- Rob started traveling as a backpacker trying to build startups. He says he had no idea what he was doing, made lots of mistakes and failures, and earned nothing for about a year.
- At first he moved every few days or every week, then every two weeks, then every month.
- He learned the hard way that moving constantly makes it very hard to focus on one thing. While building SuperX he moved non-stop and got "bits and bobs" done.
- He only got real work done after settling in Colombia for 3 months straight in July 2025.
- For roughly the last 6 months (as of this video), he sets up base somewhere for 2 to 3 months, ideally 3, then moves on.
- He finds this the right balance: routine for deep work, plus the travel.
- He believes going somewhere else to see how other people live, how money moves and what opportunities exist is "the best thing anyone can do", and that getting out and moving was the best thing he has done.

chunks.heading: Productivity follows happiness, not discipline
chunks.text:
- Rob once thought the gap between what he had and what he wanted was discipline. He thought he needed to wake earlier, plan better and lock in harder, because self-help content says so.
- Having lived in more than 13 countries in a few years, he found the places where he shipped the most were always the places where he was happiest, with no exception. In some places he barely touched his laptop. In others he shipped more than he had in months.
- His conclusion: "The variable was never discipline. It was how I felt in that place."
- His motto: "Productivity follows happiness." He says the best things you create come from being in a good place.
- His advice is to find the environment that puts you in your best place and work out what you enjoy.
- He draws on things he loved as a kid, such as wanting to travel the world.
- Tactic: he keeps a Rubik's Cube and mixes it up between prompts to stay in a state of play. He says approaching work in a state of play makes both life and work better.

chunks.heading: Protecting sleep and winding down
chunks.text:
- Rob needs 9 hours of sleep. He tried for a long time to get by on 8 and it didn't work for him.
- He spends about 9.5 hours in bed and sets his alarm for the time he goes to bed plus 9.5 hours.
- He protects sleep above everything else: without it he can't think creatively, can't stay motivated, and doesn't want to go to the gym. He says "everything is downstream of sleep".
- About an hour before bed he switches everything off. He reads or watches YouTube, may doomscroll a little, then turns his phone off for 30 minutes. He admits it isn't perfect but works for him.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam went from five products earning $0 to a $13K MRR SaaS (SuperX) by sharing his story on X and then using data to systemize virality. He lays out a seven-step playbook: profile foundation, one goal, a four-part content loop, copying concepts not posts, doubling down on winners, real connections, and following the platform's format.

chunks.heading: Rob's background and the failures that came before SuperX
chunks.text:
- Rob studied computer science, became a software engineer, and was laid off by his first employer. He decided he was done with corporate and started his journey on X in early 2023.
- Over the next two and a half years he built and launched five products that made "a whopping zero dollars" in total.
- He says those failures taught him three things: distribution matters, monetization matters from day one, and you should build painkillers, not vitamins.
- His biggest takeaway is that sharing the hard times along with the wins built trust in the community. He posted every struggle and failure along the way, and that led to his breakthrough.

chunks.heading: How a vulnerable viral post became a $3,000 client and a dev agency
chunks.text:
- After the five failures, money was scarce and he had made none in over a year. He posted about all of his failures, and the post got about 150,000 views on X.
- One comment on it suggested he start a development agency using his skills. He announced the agency on the momentum of that post and landed his first $3,000 client from it.
- All of his agency clients came inbound through X DMs from viral posts.
- He had no process for creating viral content, so he built one. He used AI, data and analytics to systematically create viral content on X, and made the most money of his life.
- That process led to his partnership with Tibo, the former co-founder of Tweet Hunter, who had acquired the SuperX Chrome extension. Rob built the SuperX web app, combining his analytics and content process into his "dream X growth tool".
- His view on why the vulnerable post worked: "so many people feel this way too."

chunks.heading: SuperX: the product, pricing and key numbers
chunks.text:
- SuperX shows which posts went viral, why they worked, and helps users create their own versions. Its parts:
  - **Inspiration page:** daily generated post ideas built from what is going viral now plus the user's context.
  - **Chrome extension:** works on any profile, shows top posts sortable by impressions or likes, and estimated X earnings. Users send viral concepts into SuperX to write and schedule content.
  - **SuperX Engage:** a newly released feature that walks users step by step through replying to posts from people in their community and tracks the replies in one place.
- Pricing is $29/month subscriptions, with about 450 active subscribers.
- He took the business from about $1,000 to over $13,000 MRR in four months after the public launch, growing about 25% month over month. The video quotes both $12,000 and $13,000; the $13,000 figure is his own.
- Revenue is split between Stripe and Lemon Squeezy, after a recent migration. Trial rate is about 30%, with about 60 active trials. Churn is close to 30%, and he is working to bring it down.
- About 95% of traffic and most users came from X. Since he started using SuperX properly (around April), he has held about 100,000 impressions a day, versus inconsistent impressions when he posted randomly. He reached over 34,000 followers in just over a year.
- He used SuperX to grow SuperX, which he calls living proof the system works.

chunks.heading: Rob's launch timeline and what actually drove signups
chunks.text:
- In January 2025 he made a New Year's resolution to start vlogging. A post about filming in public, written at the Amsterdam airport on the way to Rio de Janeiro, had over 1 million views when he landed. He closed his agency and began building SuperX around the same time.
- The first seven months were brutal: two hospitalizations from food poisoning (Guatemala and Colombia), constant X API changes that broke SuperX, and tens of "SuperX is down" messages every day. He kept building and posting.
- The July launch post was a standard screen recording with a breakdown of features. It got 32,000 views and 26 signups.
- He then posted a selfie of himself in front of his laptop. It got over 46,000 views and did not advertise the product, yet it drove far more signups than the launch post. It added $1,000 in MRR in 24 hours.
- He took that as a signal to keep going and applied the system built into SuperX to grow SuperX.
- His takeaway on why story beats product posts: with so much AI "slop" content, "people want to follow people. People want to follow stories." Sharing your story, personality and struggles honestly is how you build an audience.
- He also says: "You don't need followers to start. You need consistency, a story line, and a system."

chunks.heading: Rob's 7-step playbook for building an audience on X from zero
chunks.text:
1. **Set your foundation before posting.** Use a real, friendly, smiling face as the profile photo and don't change it often. Write a one-sentence bio. Pin a post with your goal or elevator pitch. His was: left my job and home to live on savings and try to build my dream SaaS to $10K a month. People who click through from the feed must instantly understand what you're doing.
2. **Pick one specific goal and document it daily.** This gives consistency (people forget you otherwise), a storyline (people follow journeys), and authenticity from sharing ups and downs, which builds trust.
3. **Run the content loop.** Content falls into four types: entertaining, educational, inspirational and convincing (selling). Post them in order, with intention:
   - Entertaining first: funny, relatable, vulnerable, or a fun tool launch. This earns engagement and warms up the algorithm.
   - Then educational or selling, pitched from goodwill, for example "here's how you grow on X with SuperX".
   - Then inspirational: screenshot the views, followers or sales and explain what it means to you (why you left your job). Write it from the heart so people root for you.
   - Repeat from the start. The loop builds trust, educates and sells without being annoying.
4. **Systemize what works with data.** Don't guess what to post. Analyze top-performing posts of successful profiles in your niche (he uses the SuperX Chrome extension, but any tool works). Copy the concept, not the post word for word, and restyle it with your personality.
5. **Double down on what works and kill what doesn't.** Track every post's performance, then find patterns in format, style and topic. For Rob, video and feature releases plus authentic moments work best. The algorithm rewards consistency. Kill underperformers, even a viral one.
6. **Build real connections.** Don't chase virality alone. Reply with real value to people you genuinely want to connect with: share experience and stories, ask thoughtful questions, and show up daily. Avoid AI-generated spam replies like "Great post". He treats many followers as real friends and has met them while traveling.
7. **Leverage what the platform wants.** X currently pushes video because it keeps people on the platform longer. Pay attention and adapt as this changes.

chunks.heading: How Rob used data to choose what to build and what to cut
chunks.text:
- Concrete example: he used SuperX to analyze what was going viral in his niche and found that a "curse for tweets" and an "algorithm simulator" were performing. He built both as SuperX features, posted a demo of them dancing, and it worked.
- His formula was to combine a proven viral concept with his own personality.
- He later removed the algorithm simulator from SuperX even though it went viral, because most users didn't use it.
- Switching from text to video format gave him 10 times the reach of text posts.
- His conclusion: it isn't about luck. It comes from consistent storytelling that builds trust, systemizing virality with data and analytics, and building intentional, real friendships. "If you do this, you won't need paid ads."

chunks.heading: Rob's tech stack, costs and building philosophy
chunks.text:
- Philosophy: pick one stack, learn it deeply, and ignore the noise. Too many people chase new technologies instead of shipping.
- Stack:
  - **Development:** Next.js, Node.js, Tailwind
  - **Database:** SQLite
  - **Data source:** X API, about $2,000 to $3,000/month
  - **AI:** OpenAI and Anthropic Claude Sonnet APIs, about $1,000/month
  - **Servers:** AWS, about $200/month
  - **Semantic search:** Zilliz Cloud for vector embeddings, for semantic similarity search on tweets, about $200/month
  - **AI coding:** Claude Code, about $200/month
  - **Demo videos:** Screen Studio, about $10/month
  - **Landing page:** Framer, about $10/month
  - **Payments and analytics:** Stripe and PostHog

chunks.heading: Rob's closing advice
chunks.text:
- His advice to his younger self: breathe, and do things with intention, not with emotion.
- Figure out what you want, cut out the noise, and then do "an insane amount of volume with intention".
- Take care of yourself. If you do all of this, "it's just a matter of time."
- He is clear that building in public is not for everyone, but if you are willing to put yourself out there and "embrace the cringe", the chances of building a successful product are much higher.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob tests Sakana's Fugu Ultra, a ~7B orchestrator that routes to frontier models, against Opus 4.8 on a one-line bug fix and a subjective design task. Result: no clear winner. Orchestration costs more on simple jobs, was cheaper and faster on the complex one, and the output fell short of the "matches Fable 5" claim.

chunks.heading: Sakana Fugu is an orchestration model, not a conventional frontier model
chunks.text:
- Rob describes Sakana Fugu (from Sakana AI Labs in Tokyo) as an orchestration model with about 7 billion parameters.
- Frontier models such as Opus 4.8, Fable 5 and GPT 5.5 are described as running on trillions of parameters.
- Fugu doesn't answer directly. It coordinates several models (e.g. GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8) behind the scenes, instructs them, judges their outputs and returns the result.
- His analogy: Fable 5 is one genius child, while Fugu Ultra is a classroom of smart kids working together.
- Sakana's marketing claims Fugu Ultra matches Fable 5 and Fable Mythos at roughly half the price, with no export-control risk. Rob notes those models are restricted from public access by US export controls.
- He flags that the claim is about capability without that regulatory risk, and decided to test it rather than trust it.

chunks.heading: Published benchmarks: strong, but not Fable-level
chunks.text:
- On SWE Bench Pro, Fugu Ultra scores 73.7 versus 69.2 for Opus 4.8, but remains below Fable 5.
- On long-context reasoning, GPT 5.5 leads with 94.8 versus 93.6 for Fugu Ultra.
- Rob says the close result is expected, since Fugu is using those frontier models underneath.
- He points out that a model trained specifically to orchestrate other models beating the best single model on some benchmarks is notable, even though it falls short of the Fable 5 comparison in the marketing.
- He stresses that all these benchmarks are run internally and reported by the producing company, which is why he ran his own independent comparison.

chunks.heading: How Rob ran the comparison
chunks.text:
- He used Vercel AI Gateway (not a paid ad, just a tool he uses) to bring external models into Claude Code. This lets him compare several models head to head in the same AI coding environment.
- He gave Opus 4.8 and Fugu Ultra identical tasks: a simple one-line bug fix, and a more complex design task he could judge subjectively.
- He tracked quality, cost, tokens used and run time.
- Setup friction: Fugu isn't available in the EU and Asia because of GDPR and data-security compliance. Rob is in Vietnam and worked around it with a VPN.
- The orchestration is invisible. He sees only the token count and the bill, not which models Fugu chose or why.
- Alternatives to AI Gateway for testing models himself: Fireworks.

chunks.heading: Test 1, simple one-line bug fix: single model wins on cost
chunks.text:
- Opus 4.8 found the bug. It cost about 14 cents, using roughly 1,500 input and 1,700 output tokens (a little over 3,000 total).
- Fugu Ultra also fixed the bug, but cost 80 cents, about 5.7x more, and used 147,000 tokens.
- Rob's read: that overhead makes sense for a model coordinating multiple agents in the background and comparing their results.
- He concedes nobody would realistically use an orchestrator for a trivial bug, which is why he added a second test.

chunks.heading: Test 2, complex design task (a "kebab stand" HTML design benchmark)
chunks.text:
- The task asks a model to produce an HTML kebab design, scored subjectively. Rob credits GLM 5.2, an open-source model, as the best open-source result on this benchmark, in his view.
- Opus 4.8: about $2.55, around 15 minutes, a little over 70,000 tokens (6,000 input, 64,000 output). Result: a rotating 3D kebab with fire in the background, glow, and fat dripping into a pool at the bottom. He was very happy with it.
- Fugu Ultra: about 50 cents, roughly 4 minutes (about a third of the time), 35.8k input and 12k output tokens. It produced a valid HTML file.
- Quality: Rob was disappointed. The output was 2D with little detail and only simple animation. A "drag to direct heat" prompt did nothing when clicked, which he attributes to multiple orchestrated models not communicating with each other.
- It was better than GLM 5.1 and GLM 5, but he found GLM 5.2 (open source, much cheaper) clearly more impressive.
- He says he expected far better, given the claim that Fugu rivals Fable 5, and the gap with Opus 4.8 should have been large if that were true.

chunks.heading: Rob's verdict: no clear winner, so pick by task and cost
chunks.text:
- Simple tasks: a single model (Opus 4.8) gets the same result far more cheaply.
- Complex, creative tasks: Fugu was cheaper and faster but lower quality in his test.
- He doesn't want the kebab test to be the only takeaway. Sakana's bet is that orchestration models are the future of AI, and he thinks that bet is interesting, especially with export controls on frontier models.
- Orchestration adds a layer that extracts and coordinates the best of several models, but it comes at a cost: either lower performance at much lower cost, or equal-or-better results on some benchmarks (like SWE Bench Pro, which he didn't test) at a much higher price.
- Practical advice: in most cases, stick with one model and your current workflow, since it's cheaper and more sensible. The landscape could change in a week or two.
- "Don't just take my word for it, try it yourself." He recommends spending a little money to test models on your own workload, because everyone's needs differ, and invites viewers to report if their results differ.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob traces his path from laid-off software engineer to co-founding SuperX. After a year of $0 revenue he launched an agency off a viral tweet to get cash flow and runway, then built a product from his own itch. He explains why founders should test many channels and double down where fit, enjoyment and a painful problem align.

chunks.heading: From zero income to an agency to SuperX
chunks.text:
- Rob studied computer science and became a software engineer in 2022, based in Reading, UK. He took the traditional path but disliked the job: isolated, overworking, no friends nearby, bad weather. He calls it "the closest I was to being depressed."
- He was laid off in November 2022 with a small pay package and took it as a sign to go all in on building his own thing. He looked at e-commerce, dropshipping and SaaS.
- In 2023 he joined a small startup through a friend. It ran out of money, partly through poor management.
- Seeing Marc Lou make millions through his X audience with ShipFast showed him "there's another world out there."
- In September 2023 he began "indie hacking" and sharing publicly on X. His first product was Indie Index (a directory of indie hackers). A tweet asking who'd want it got about 50 likes, when he had around 100 followers, so he treated it as validation. It took about 4 months to ship.
- Indie Index did not make money because he never monetized it. His lesson: "you need a buy button on something to be able to take people's money otherwise it's not a business."

chunks.heading: Solving cash flow with an agency
chunks.text:
- Rob's core early-stage problem was cash flow. Without it you either work a job and build on weekends, or you're short on both cash and time.
- After launching Indie Index he made $0 for a full year while backpacking and building. He tweeted that he'd made no money in 12 months and offered himself as a freelance developer.
- A reply suggested he sell his skills as an agency rather than freelance, so he spun one up off the back of that viral tweet and launched immediately.
- He landed his first client for $3,000 for one month. It was the first money he'd made in a year, and it compounded from there.
- The agency gave him both validation and runway.
- His advice for new builders: either keep a job and build on the side until it pays enough to quit, or run an agency (as he did) to build runway.
- He applied the same pattern recently with Can I Vibe Code?: take the momentum of a viral tweet and launch immediately.

chunks.heading: Marketing: get in front of your ICP and test many channels
chunks.text:
- Rob defines marketing as getting in front of people, specifically the right people (your ideal customer profile).
- His channel for Indie Index and the agency was X, where his audience (indie hackers) already lived. All his agency clients came inbound: he posted wins, people DM'd, they booked a meeting, he signed them, then posted about that to attract more.
- He says X works for him because sharing his journey feels natural and fits his ICP. He also notes he prefers the marketing side over "being in the weeds coding."
- Options he lists:
  - SEO (dying, turning into AEO). Cheap but slow to compound.
  - Outreach. Works for some, for example Goji Berry (about $4M a year) does outreach plus X and ads.
  - Ads, if you have cash flow, which many indie hackers lack.
  - Building in public. The downside is that anything that works gets copied if you lack a moat. Mobile app founders often have the viral content format as their moat, so sharing it gets it ripped off.
- He cites Nevo (Postiz) that what worked two years ago doesn't work today.
- He doesn't think one channel fits everyone. When starting, he says to try as many channels as you can and see which works.
- His formula for doubling down: a painful enough problem, a marketing channel that works, and something you enjoy enough to stay motivated. Indies work alone, so self-motivation matters. When those three line up, "it just cascades."
- He does not recommend using AI to automate your personality on X.

chunks.heading: How SuperX came about
chunks.text:
- While running the agency, Rob wanted a tool to help craft tweets and learn what goes viral by analyzing data. Existing tools like Tweet Hunter hadn't integrated AI yet.
- He built a product to scratch his own itch, knowing the market was validated because competitors existed. He called it Brandcast.
- During competitor analysis he found SuperX, a Chrome extension. A few months later Tibo (now his co-founder) acquired it from the original founder, and the collaboration with that founder didn't work out, so Tibo took full ownership and posted looking for a co-founder.
- Rob sent Tibo a Loom of Brandcast, they worked together for a week, then agreed to partner.
- It then took about 6 months of grind before SuperX started working. The title claims $20K+/month.
- Rob credits luck for the opportunity but says he acted on it: the chain ran from the $0 year to the agency, the itch, Brandcast, Tibo's tweet, and the grind. His takeaway is to keep going because you never know when something will work.

chunks.heading: Lifestyle and location notes
chunks.text:
- Rob lives as a digital nomad. He calls Thailand his favorite country: safe, modern, excellent hospitals and infrastructure, cafes with 300-400 Mbps Wi-Fi, mountains and beaches, and cheap, beautiful scuba diving in Koh Tao.
- He applied for Thailand's DTV (a five-year visa allowing six-month stays) and is currently in Vietnam.
- He found Latin America (Brazil, Colombia, Guatemala, Panama) enjoyable but felt more on edge there because of safety.
- He recommends Southeast Asia as a starting point for travelers, and Vietnam and Chiang Mai for settling long term. He says he's past the stage of moving somewhere new every two weeks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Hallam walks through a layoff, several unmonetized side projects, an MVP agency fueled by X posts, and a partnership that became SuperX. He teaches validating with buy buttons, sharing wins and losses publicly, and iterating through high volume while learning from each failed attempt.

chunks.heading: Path to a first SaaS: wins, losses, and volume
chunks.text:
- Rob graduated in computer science in the UK and worked as a low-level software engineer at a video conferencing company, fixing bugs in protocols.
- He says he never enjoyed it and felt like an imposter because he is creative and loves the arts rather than deep programming.
- He was laid off and treats it as a positive: paid to leave with about two months, plus a runway to experiment.
- His mindset line: "Optimists will always win."
- A friend in a crypto startup told him what to learn: Next.js, Node.js, JavaScript, Tailwind.
- He learned them from a YouTube Next.js course (about 20 videos) in roughly a month, then worked nine months at that startup until it went bust at the end of 2023.
- Building a real app taught him far more than watching tutorials.

chunks.heading: Early failed products and what each taught him
chunks.text:
- Rob was inspired by Marc Lou's ShipFast (Next.js boilerplate) and flew to Egypt in September 2023 to build with his friend Mustafa.
- Failure 1: a software agency with friends, "Techia".
- Failure 2: Coach Miro, connecting coaches with coaches.
- Failure 3: Indidex (indidex.app), a "Pokedex for indie hackers", a directory of indie hackers pulled from X.
  - Validation: he tweeted the idea, got about 2,000 views when his posts normally got 20-30, then shipped an MVP in a few days.
  - Launched on Product Hunt in March 2024 and got #4, 100,000 impressions on launch day, 250 users, and no monetization.
- Failure 4: Pentest List, a directory of ethical hacking tools, built in two weeks for a family friend who is a pentester.
  - The plan was to monetize with ads, which he calls naive because ads need a lot of traffic.
  - It gets about 1,000-1,500 visits a month (about 50 a day), all from SEO, and made no money. It taught him SEO as a distribution channel.
- Takeaways he draws:
  - Building what he found cool but nobody would pay for kept repeating.
  - Review each failure, ask what went well and wrong, and fix it next time ("The lesson will keep repeating itself until you've learned from it").
  - His fixes in order: distribution (SEO, X), then monetization (a buy button, then an agency for runway).

chunks.heading: Validation: interest versus money
chunks.text:
- Rob separates interest validation (people click and look) from monetary validation (people pay).
- Indidex had interest but no money. He had not monetized anything early, which he attributes to imposter syndrome or fear of using Stripe.
- "People saying that they would pay money doesn't mean they're going to pay money." The best test is putting a buy link on the product.
- Go to where your customers are (indie hackers were on X), post the idea or a teaser, and measure the interest.
- Visual demos spread well, as with the "I built cursor for X" style posts.

chunks.heading: The Liftoff MVP agency funded by building in public
chunks.text:
- Rob posted a long tweet with a selfie (about August 2024) saying he had made "$0" in 11 months of savings, listing his four failures and what each taught him.
- Peter Levels replied that 26 more failures and he would statistically be a winner, which motivated him. Ian Nuttle suggested a service charging $2,000-$5,000 to ship an MVP, with an optional monthly retainer.
- Within 24 hours Rob launched an MVP-building service called Liftoff. Within about a week of the post he signed his first client at $3,000.
- Over about four months, deals grew: $3,000, then $5,000 (a couple), then $6,000, and finally two clients on back-to-back days worth $18,000 combined.
- Every client came inbound from X. They arrived already sold because they had seen his wins, losses, and proof.
- His method for those months: post everything (each client signed, each hire, each problem). Losses and struggles resonate with more people than wins, which are merely inspirational.
- Post yourself: a selfie or face content stands out against AI-generated text.
- He cites the "digital gravity" analogy (from Cody Schneider's circle): each piece of content adds mass to your personal brand, so customers orbit several times before they "land" and buy.
- He wound the agency down in December 2024 because of client complaints and contractor issues, and because it was unfulfilling and stressful ("a hedonistic treadmill"). Agency work trades time for money.

chunks.heading: From using AI for his own tweets to SuperX
chunks.text:
- A fellow MVP agency owner told Rob he keeps one long ChatGPT conversation that learns his voice and uses it to write tweets. Rob tried it, tweaked the output, and got several tweets to go viral.
- Stance on AI slop: AI turns good ideas or good writing into great writing. Slop comes from bad ideas and low effort ("Garbage in, garbage out").
- He decided to productize it as an app, "Brancast" (broadcast your brand), and bought the domain. The first version was messy and niche to his own use.
- He asked Tibo (a SuperX co-founder) for private beta access to SuperX. The product was janky but had a user base and a Chrome extension with validation and data.
- In January 2025 Tibo posted that SuperX's technical co-founder collaboration was ending and he was seeking a new one. Rob sent a Loom of what he had built, saying he would otherwise compete. He built the SuperX web app in about a week, and they started working together.
- SuperX began as a Chrome extension for X analytics. The web app helps users write, plan, and schedule posts and generate content ideas.
- Rob's vision: speak an idea and have the tweet, images, and scheduling handled, with a content strategist chat that reads your analytics and explains what to change.
- He also shipped an "AI Shield" feature: the extension scans each tweet in the feed and scores 0-10 for how likely it is AI-written (em dashes, overly optimistic tone). Users can hide or label content over a threshold.

chunks.heading: SuperX launch and numbers
chunks.text:
- Over about six months, SuperX grew to $1,600 MRR in private beta with roughly 30 active web app users. Private beta users also paid, covering AI and server costs.
- He got those users by screen-recording or screenshotting features and posting "reply SuperX for early access", then DMing a link to those who replied.
- Soft launch of the web app was on Wednesday the 9th (July 2025), with harder launches planned later (more videos, Product Hunt) after a couple of weeks of feedback.
- Launch method: one tweet with a short video (an old extension demo clip stitched with a screen recording, edited in DaVinci with music), then follow-up progress updates, wins, losses, and selfies to keep momentum.
- The launch tweet got about 30,000 views and 100 likes ("semi-viral"). In 24-36 hours it brought about 50 free-trial signups at $29/month on a 7-day trial. He expected MRR to rise from about $1.6K to roughly $2.5K, assuming around a 50% trial conversion.

chunks.heading: Principles for persistence and finding what works
chunks.text:
- Core idea: "The more you do, the more you find out." Do more, ship more, and follow the leads that appear, like buying more lottery tickets.
- Changing his physical environment helped him break out of a stuck period (he went from Koh Samui to the UK for a month).
- Quote he credits to Alex Hormozi (as "Homozy"): figure out what you want, clear out all your distractions, and do so much volume that it is statistically improbable you will fail.
- Cut distractions: limit TikTok and reels, avoid constantly watching how others are doing, since you don't see their full picture.
- Keep a personal "why" strong enough to sustain volume. His is supporting his family, who backed him throughout, and avoiding health and money worries.
- Surround yourself with people who share your values, and drift away from those who criticize the path.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob explains how he went from a failed year to $14k MRR by building SuperX with Tibo Maker, using public build-in-public content on X. He covers a 90-day X growth framework, the 80/20 focus lesson, churn feedback, viral feature ideas, and the max-MRR math behind his $100k goal.

chunks.heading: Starting point and the leap to Rio
chunks.text:
- Rob spent roughly August 2023 to August 2024 making no money and burning savings. A tweet about that failed year went viral.
- A commenter suggested he start a development agency. He launched it the next day and landed a $3,000 client from a follow-up post.
- He kept posting client wins on X and got more clients inbound. The agency built the savings that let him quit and fly to Rio de Janeiro in January 2025.
- His takeaway: "there's money on X", whether through an agency or something else.
- He had about 3,500-4,000 followers before the Rio video. That one video added about 5,000 followers in 24 hours, roughly double what he'd built in a year and a half.
- His pinned post stated a goal: "My goal is to build a SaaS business to $10,000 a month and to document the process." It stayed pinned for a year, so visitors could follow the story to the goal.

chunks.heading: Growing on X: profile, pin post and the 4-part content loop
chunks.text:
- Profile first. Use a real, friendly picture of yourself and never change it, because AI slop and bots are the main competition. Keep the bio to one or two lines on what you're doing.
- The pin post is an elevator pitch: who you are, what you're building, and the goal you've committed to for the next 90 days.
- He rotates through four content types:
  1. Entertaining (viral demos, vlogs, memes) warms you up in the algorithm.
  2. Educational (threads, how-tos) gets served to the people who engaged with the entertaining post.
  3. Convincing (selling), placed authentically at the end of the educational content, e.g. "SuperX is free to try for 7 days".
  4. Inspirational (screenshots of results and what they mean to you), tied back to your pin post story.
- Then loop back to entertaining. He argues a framework stops you posting randomly, which is why people drop off.
- Do cool things first; the content follows from them. His dancing feature demos only existed because he built the feature.
- He notes that top-of-funnel entertainment with selling at the end is how most big content earners make money.

chunks.heading: Treating X like a room: engagement and authenticity
chunks.text:
- Engagement pods with friends are a good idea. Otherwise, treat X as a huge networking party: don't shout from the rooftops; go person to person, listen, and join conversations on your interests.
- Treat early interactions as friendships, not transactions. He met Florian, Mark Lou, Tony Dinh, Jack Friks and others this way, and says most friends he meets in person now came from X.
- On authenticity: he cites Robert Greene's view that authenticity is a performance. His practical version:
  - Pick inspirations and copy them at first, then add your own take. Mine were Marc Lou (filming in public), Daniel Dalen (video style) and Peter Levels (raw, opinionated, unfiltered).
  - Authenticity comes from discovering what you genuinely enjoy and releasing pressure about the result.
  - Share a bit of what's in your head as it happens, e.g. "I was genuinely crapping myself in the airport".
- He loved making videos and chasing the algorithm since childhood (YouTube at 10, a meme channel at 15-16). He says combining your own skills makes you distinct.
- He warns against turning passion into pressure: after his first YouTube video hit 125,000 views, he burned out on the second.

chunks.heading: Consistency, the daily video and the minimum viable video
chunks.text:
- Consistency works like escape velocity for a rocket: pauses cost you more than they save, especially early. People forget you within 24-48 hours.
- Appear online daily, but you don't have to create daily. Schedule content: spend an hour on Monday scheduling seven days of tweets.
- Scheduling can't capture real-time opinions on trends, so mix it with live posting.
- He posted a daily video documenting SuperX growth from about $1,000/month to $10,000/month, taking about 131 days. Afterwards he went weekly because daily videos burn a lot of energy.
- Minimum viable video: on bad days (he was in hospital with food poisoning and neck issues in Colombia) he filmed a quick clip, put a song and a caption over it, and still posted.
- The daily video helped SuperX because it showed an involved founder, and people started recognizing his face in person.
- Daily doing something others won't (like Mr Beast's endurance challenges) makes you stand out.

chunks.heading: What works in the X algorithm (as of Dec 2025)
chunks.text:
- X rewards time on platform. His feed is dominated by media posts and quote tweets, so video or images plus text is what gets seen.
- Winning format: media plus a long, honest opinion that invites debate. His Singapore posts (video or photo plus long text) got 607,000, 574,000, 181,000 and 73,000 views, with a post the day before at 133,000.
- Post unfiltered, as if in a group chat.
- Opinions must be real. Intentional rage-baiting or engagement farming loses integrity and brings haters; he got death threats from some posts.
- Evergreen concepts resurface: a repost two or three months later with your own spin goes viral again, because "two or three months is like 200 years on the internet".
- He runs experiments on his own profile constantly.

chunks.heading: Taking over SuperX and rebuilding it
chunks.text:
- SuperX began as a Chrome extension built by Hugh. Tibo Maker (Tweet Hunter and Taplio exit) acquired it, raised prices and wanted a web app. Hugh left and Tibo took the remaining shares.
- Tibo posted for a full-stack maker. Rob was closing his agency and had been building a similar tool called Brandcast, so he applied with a proof of concept.
- His one-week trial was building an AI tweet inspirations feature, built during his week in Rio. Tibo chose him over the other finalist. They work async over Slack with no video calls since January.
- The inherited product: five repositories, four EC2 instances, a Chrome extension, an SEO server and a vector-embedding server for similarity search. He had to learn and build CI/CD for each.
- Migrations he had to do:
  - X API v1 to v2, and repeated changes since (including pay-per-usage).
  - Vector database (Milvus) off Docker to the cloud when load grew.
  - Media uploads moved to Cloudflare R2.
  - OAuth 1 to OAuth 2, with token syncing between extension and web app.
  - Lemon Squeezy to Stripe. Subscriptions had to be recreated manually, and the right card per subscription copied. A first batch failed, costing MRR, and he emailed users directly.
- From January to July 2025 he earned about $1,500 total, with MRR hovering between $600 and $1,000-1,200. He says he doubted nearly every day, as "I'll put out a fire here and 10 other fires will ignite".
